title: Parties in Palauan
bodyHtml:
Palau is a country in the Pacific Ocean composed of eight islands and over 200 islets. In addition to English, the Austronesian language Palauan is an official language of Palau. Below are some noun phrases from the Palauan language, with their English translations:

PalauanEnglish
eru ęl builtwo months
ede ęl silsthree days
tede ęl chadthree people
kllolem ęl malksix chickens
teim ęl senseifive teachers
eim ęl rakfive years
etiu ęl klębęsenine nights
kltiu ęl hongnine books
kllolem ęl liussix coconuts
teai ęl ngalękeight children
tęruich me a tede ęl buikthirteen boys
tęruich me a euid ęl sikangseventeen hours
ongeru ęl builFebruary
ongede ęl ureorWednesday

Answer the following questions below.

questions.promptHtml: b. tęruich me a etiu ęl buil
c. ongetęruich me a ongeru ęl buil

questions.answerKey: tęruich me a tetiu ęl chad
acceptedVariants: teruich me a tetiu el chad

questions.partPrompt: For each of the following phrases, write the Palauan word that would be used to translate the bolded word:

hints.text: Compare the number words for the same numeral across different rows: "five teachers" and "five years" do not use the same word for "five", and neither does "six chickens" match the shape of "three days". Look at what comes at the start of each number word, and what kind of thing is being counted.

Each numeral has a bare stem plus a prefix chosen by the class of noun it counts: one prefix for units of time, another for people, another for animals, fruits and certain objects. Teens are built as the word for ten, then me a, then the ones digit carrying the right prefix. A separate prefix turns a cardinal number into an ordinal ("second", "third"), which is how month names and weekday names are made.

Work an example that is not asked about: "nine nights" is etiu ęl klębęse and "nine books" is kltiu ęl hong, so the stem for nine is -tiu, taking e- with a time unit and kl- with a book. That means "nine chickens" would be kltiu ęl malk, and "nine people" would take the people prefix on the same stem instead.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: The same numeral, several shapes

Line up the rows that share a numeral. "five teachers" is teim ęl sensei but "five years" is eim ęl rak. Both contain -im; the difference is the piece in front: te- before a word for people, nothing extra (just e-) before a unit of time. Do the same for nine: etiu ęl klębęse "nine nights" versus kltiu ęl hong "nine books". Again the stem is shared (-tiu) and the prefix changes.

Step 2: The three prefixes

A noun class is a group of nouns that a language treats the same way grammatically. Palauan numbers pick their prefix from the class of the noun being counted:

  • e- for units of time (months, days, years, nights, hours)
  • te- for people (teachers, boys, children, people)
  • kl- for animals, fruits and some inanimate objects (chickens, coconuts, books)

So from ede ęl sils "three days" and tede ęl chad "three people" we can read off the stem for three, and from kllolem ęl malk / kllolem ęl lius we get six in the animal-and-object shape. The little word ęl just links the number to the noun.

Step 3: Numbers above ten

tęruich me a tede ęl buik is "thirteen boys" and tęruich me a euid ęl sikang is "seventeen hours". So a teen is tęruich (ten) + me a + the ones digit, and it is the ones digit that carries the class prefix: tede (people class) with boys, euid (time class) with hours. To say "nineteen months" you therefore keep the time-class nine; to say "nineteen people" you swap in the people-class nine.

Step 4: Ordinals, months and weekdays

ongeru ęl buil means February and ongede ęl ureor means Wednesday. Notice -ru (two) and -de (three): February is literally "second month" and Wednesday is "third day". The extra piece onge- is the ordinal marker, so onge- plus a number gives "second", "third", "fifth", and so on. Month names are that ordinal plus buil "month"; weekday names are the ordinal plus ureor. Counting from Sunday as day one, the third day is Wednesday, so the fifth day lands on Friday.

Two details fall out of this. First, sils and ureor both translate as "day", but sils is the 24-hour unit of time while ureor is a named day of the week. Second, for an ordinal above ten the onge- marker attaches to the "ten" part as well, which is why a form like ongetęruich me a ongeru reads as "twelfth" and, with buil, names the twelfth month.

Step 5: Answering E3

E3 only asks for the number word, so all you need is the class of the noun after it: hours are a unit of time, girls are people, and dolphins are animals. Take the stem for three that you extracted in Step 2 and attach the matching prefix from the list above.
